idiom_name: transformer object/function per domain type writing to an output sink (or one stylesheet per channel)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give each domain type (or output format) one transformer whose single operation receives the model and writes the markup element by element to an output sink it does not own; keep the transformer stateless and free of request, session and database access so it can be unit-tested and reused by any caller. When the platform provides an XSLT processor and the domain is already XML, the transformer becomes a stylesheet applied by the processor, with per-request values passed as parameters and compiled stylesheets cached. In both forms, centralize output escaping, factor shared page furniture into reusable fragments or a logical page, and stream to the response when documents are large.

pitfalls: Letting the transformer read request/session state or fetch data destroys reusability and testability.
Hand-rolled escaping applied inconsistently: one missed text or attribute write is enough to inject markup.
Building the whole document in memory when the sink could be streamed to.

Wrong move: writing stylesheets against XSLT 2.0/3.0 features or browser-side rendering -> deployment against an XSLT 1.0 processor fails (browsers only ever implemented 1.0, and Chrome removes XSLTProcessor and xml-stylesheet outright in late 2026) -> instead transform server-side on a processor you control and pin stylesheets to the XSLT version that processor implements.

Wrong move: binding stylesheet templates directly to the domain-object serialization -> a domain refactor changes the serialized shape and rendering breaks silently -> instead bind stylesheets to a stable logical presentation format (the Two Step View) or version the serialization contract.

Wrong move: one flat stylesheet of global template rules shared across pages -> a rule added for one page matches another page's elements and output breaks far from the edit -> instead scope transformations into per-page stylesheets or modes, or move tangled dispatch logic into host-language transformers.
